about: SIMULATED, hand-authored. This is NOT a recorded model run and must never be transcribed into docs/internal/eval-runs/eval-runs.md as a measured cell. It exists so the F3 harness has a fixed input whose partition is known by construction: a near-ideal frontier review of the seeded-defect fixture that catches every auto-scorable planted defect, states the semantic entry correctly (which still lands in adjudication, because the key refuses to auto-credit it), makes no false claim, and adds one out-of-scope house-scaffolding recommendation. Expected against privacy-notice-toolkit.key.json 1.0.0: precision 1.00, recall 0.89 PROVISIONAL (8 of 9, the auto ceiling; SD-06 is review-required).

findings.message: dsar-intake-triage and data-request-router have colliding trigger surfaces. Both descriptions fire on an inbound access, deletion, correction, or opt-out request, both classify it by type, both assign an owner, and both stamp the same 45-day deadline. Asked to handle an arriving deletion request, an agent has no basis to prefer one. Each description reads well on its own, which is why nothing per-component sees it.
findings.recommendation: Narrow one surface explicitly: dsar-intake-triage owns intake and verification, data-request-router owns queue assignment, and each description names the other. Merging them is the other acceptable fix.

findings.message: The manifest declares an agent at ./agents/notice-reviewer.md. No such file is on disk: the agent that ships is agents/privacy-reviewer.md, which is also the name the README uses. The declared path resolves to nothing, so the manifest catalogues something it cannot deliver.
findings.recommendation: Point the declaration at ./agents/privacy-reviewer.md, or drop the agents array and let the agents directory be discovered.

findings.message: Section 4 documents a --write flag that writes the redline back over the source notice. The skill removed that capability: its own changelog records '0.3.0 - removed the in-place write. The review now returns a report and never edits the source notice', and the four-step procedure has no write step. The reference is stale and points a reader at a flag that no longer exists.
findings.recommendation: Delete section 4, or replace it with a line stating that the review returns a report and never edits the source notice.

findings.message: Step 3 computes expires_at from granted_at alone. The skill's own schema reference states the opposite rule: a renewal restarts the retention clock, and the window runs from renewed_at when that column is populated. Every renewed consent is therefore reported as expired, so the audit tells the team to re-collect consent it already holds and an assessment reading the output would record a compliance failure that did not happen.
findings.recommendation: Compute the deadline from renewed_at when it is populated and from granted_at otherwise, matching the documented retention clock.

findings.message: The Colorado row cites a 'Colorado Consumer Data Protection Act (CCDPA)'. No statute of that name exists. Colorado's consumer privacy statute is the Colorado Privacy Act, SB 21-190. The rest of the row is accurate, which is what makes the invented name easy to read past: that law did take effect on July 1, 2023, and its response clock is 45 days with one 45-day extension.
findings.recommendation: Cite the row as Colorado Privacy Act, SB 21-190, and leave the in-force date and the deadline as they are.

findings.message: The 'Direction of consent' section states both regimes backwards. Under the GDPR, with the ePrivacy rules, direct marketing email to an individual generally needs prior opt-in consent rather than an objection route bolted onto unsolicited mail. Colorado and Virginia run the other way: targeted advertising carries a consumer right to opt out, and Colorado additionally requires honouring a universal opt-out signal. The section itself warns that mixing the two up is the most common drafting error, and then does it.
findings.recommendation: State the GDPR side as prior opt-in consent for direct marketing email, and the two state regimes as an opt-out right for targeted advertising, noting that consent for sensitive data is a separate rule.

findings.message: The command says it runs skills/privacy-notice-review and then publishes its own seven-point checklist. Both are presented as canonical and both have seven items, but only two are shared: categories of personal data collected, and consumer rights and how to exercise them. The other five in the command (a cookie banner, a reading level, sale and sharing disclosure, a named data protection officer, a review date) appear nowhere in the skill, and five of the skill's items appear nowhere in the command. A user running the command gets a verdict table the skill would never produce.
findings.recommendation: Delete the command's enumeration and point at the skill's, which the skill declares canonical, or reconcile the two into one list held in one place.

findings.message: The README says the notice review 'generates a signed PDF compliance certificate and emails it to your DPO once the review closes clean'. Nothing in the plugin can do either: there is no MCP server, no hook, no script and no dependency, and all four skills state that they return Markdown into the conversation. This is a capability overclaim, and it is the one promise a buyer would rely on, since it is the only artifact the toolkit says leaves the conversation.
findings.recommendation: Delete the sentence, or move it to a roadmap section marked clearly as not implemented.

findings.message: The per-state deadlines section points at ../skills/privacy-notice-review/references/state-law-matrix.md. That file is absent; the reference in that directory is us-state-laws.md, so the link is dead for anyone who follows it.
The plugin ships no library.json and no AGENTS.md, so a reader has no machine-readable inventory and no agent-facing entry point.
findings.recommendation: Adopt the house scaffolding if this plugin is going to be maintained alongside askit libraries.

insights: The deterministic gate reports 0 errors and 0 warnings on this target, so everything above is a judgment finding by construction.
Two of the nine (the fake statute and the inverted consent direction) are knowledge-content defects: they read as authoritative and only a reader who checks the law can see them.
